09-1.title: Supervisor vs peer-to-peer
09-1.tldr: A supervisor is one controller that plans and dispatches to workers (workers-as-tools), top-down; peer-to-peer has agents share a board/bus and coordinate as equals.

09-2.title: Multi-agent communication
09-2.tldr: Either a shared blackboard (task board/state) plus a message bus, or direct messaging; messages should be persisted and ordered for auditability, with routing (direct/broadcast/mentions).

09-3.title: Agent output as another's input
09-3.tldr: Either a call returns the value (subagent/tool), a handoff transfers control and context, or a shared board/bus carries the artifact — the framework must define result and context propagation.

09-4.title: Conflicting/redundant results
09-4.tldr: Give each unit of work one owner, enforce one-active-task-per-worker, arbitrate claims atomically, reassign instead of release, dedupe dispatch, and isolate workspaces.

09-5.title: Debugging a multi-agent failure
09-5.tldr: You need per-agent attribution: a trace/span tree where every agent, model, and tool call is a span with agent identity, plus durable conversation/task history to reconstruct order.

09-6.title: When multi-agent is overkill
09-6.tldr: Multi-agent is justified when workstreams are genuinely independent, scopes differ (tools/permissions), or specialization would otherwise fight for one context; otherwise a single well-designed agent is simpler.
points: Otherwise: a single agent is simpler.
